title: Houthis Hit 2 Saudi Oil Tankers as US Strikes Iran for 12th Night — Hormuz Frozen Since July 15
excerpt: Two Saudi oil tankers hit in the Red Sea as the US-Iran war enters night 12. No tankers through Hormuz since July 15. What happens when both critical shipping lanes go dark simultaneously?
content:
Yemen's Houthi rebels said on July 23 that they attacked two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea — the first strikes since the group announced a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia just three days earlier.

The Houthis said they targeted the tankers Encelia and Layla with drones and missiles, accusing them of violating the blockade announced on July 20. Saudi Arabia's state news agency confirmed that the Encelia was struck, with a fire breaking out at the bow of the vessel.

The attack escalates an already severe crisis in the region. The United States completed its 12th consecutive night of airstrikes against Iran on July 22, part of a campaign that began on July 11 in response to Iranian attacks on commercial shipping at the Strait of Hormuz. US President Donald Trump said Washington would hold Iran responsible for any future Houthi attacks.

Iran has retaliated against the US campaign, striking targets in Kuwait and Jordan. According to Iran's Ministry of Health, at least 53 people in Iran have been killed since US strikes began on July 11, with nearly 600 others injured.

The effects on global shipping have been immediate. According to data analytics firm Kpler, no tankers have passed through the Strait of Hormuz since July 15. The Strait of Hormuz is the world's single most important oil shipping chokepoint, handling roughly 20% of global oil trade under normal conditions.

Oil prices have reacted sharply. Brent crude is trading around $89 per barrel, having surged past $100 per barrel earlier in 2026 when the conflict first escalated. Each new round of attacks on tankers or military targets pushes prices higher again.

The Houthi naval blockade against Saudi Arabia opens a second pressure point. Saudi Arabia exports millions of barrels of oil daily, and has diverted some shipments through its East-West Pipeline to a terminal on the Red Sea coast — reducing, but not eliminating, the disruption.

The Bab al-Mandeb Strait — the southern entrance to the Red Sea — sits under Houthi threat, while the Strait of Hormuz to the east remains frozen by US-Iran hostilities. Two of the world's most critical shipping lanes, both under simultaneous pressure, represent a level of disruption that markets and governments have rarely had to manage at the same time.

Trump's statement linking Houthi actions directly to Iranian responsibility signals that further US escalation against Tehran remains on the table, depending on whether the attacks on Saudi targets continue. See also: how US intelligence technology is shaping modern military operations.
